# Ayakūṭajātaka (Ja 347)

**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Ayakūṭajātaka* (Ja 347) is a canonical birth story in the Pali *Jātaka* collection [SuttaCentral]. According to the narrative framework, the Buddha delivered this teaching while staying at Jetavana regarding the duty of acting for the welfare of the world (*lokatthacariya*), with its introductory circumstances linked to the *Mahākaṇha-jātaka* [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883]. The story of the past opens with the Bodhisatta born as a prince to the chief queen of King Brahmadatta in Bārāṇasī [Fausböll 1883]. Upon ascending the throne, the Bodhisatta issues a royal decree outlawing animal sacrifice and non-virtuous offerings of meat, blood, and alcohol to spirits (*yakkhas* and *devatās*) [Sutherland 1991; DeCaroli 2004]. Deprived of their offerings, a council of enraged *yakkhas* meeting in the Himalayas dispatches a fierce demon—described as calling himself a *rakṣa*—to execute the king with a weapon [Sutherland 1991; DeCaroli 2004; Schönberger 2012]. Although the king cannot physically defend himself against the demonic assassin, the moral power generated by his nonviolent governance commands the attention of Sakka (Indra), who appears from the heavens, shields the Bodhisatta, and drives off the attacker with a vow of lasting protection [Sutherland 1991; DeCaroli 2004].
Modern scholarship discusses this narrative primarily in the context of the Buddhist assimilation of indigenous Indian spirit cults. Robert DeCaroli observes that the *Ayakūṭajātaka*, like the *Dummedhajātaka*, reflects a monastic strategy to purge popular spirit worship of violent and intoxicant-laden practices rather than attempting to abolish the worship of *yakkhas* altogether [DeCaroli 2004]. Gail Hinich Sutherland underscores how the Bodhisatta's ethical transcendence over the sacrificial cult subordinates both popular *yakkhas* and Vedic deities like Indra, whose protective assistance is compelled by the Bodhisatta's righteousness [Sutherland 1991].
Regarding textual parallels and reuse, SuttaCentral lists four translations across modern languages but records no direct external parallels [SuttaCentral]. Computational analysis by DharmaNexus similarly identifies no cross-language matches in Chinese, Sanskrit, or Tibetan corpora, while detecting substantial Pali-internal text reuse with the commentary in the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Tatiyo bhāgo, §1.4–4.4) [DharmaNexus]. The canonical verse begins with the opening lemma *Sabbāyasaṃ* [Fausböll 1883].
